AGENTS.md

Source: AGENTS.md

Notes for AI coding agents working on ocean3d. Read CONTRIBUTING.md for the general contribution process and SPEC.md for the package design; this file covers conventions agents tend to get wrong. When the workflow changes, update this file in the same PR.

Data models

ocean3d currently has two data models for gridded data (see SPEC.md, “Data model”): netCDF files read with ncdf4 (extract_to_point(), extract_to_buffer(), extract_to_track()) and SpatVoxel / SpatEnvelope objects built on terra (everything else). #99 plans to unify them.

  • Check which model a function takes before passing data to it or adding to it, and say which one in its @param docs.
  • Don’t add a third representation or a new conversion between the two without checking SPEC.md and #99 first. New work should fit the planned model, not widen the split.
  • Each analysis function belongs to one step: build, intersect or summarise (SPEC.md, “Package design”). Add new features to one step; don’t add another function that does all three in one call.

Reuse before you write

Build on the functions and data representations the package already has before adding new ones.

  • Before writing a helper, search R/ for one that already does the job (reading bounds, detecting variables, decoding time, summarising a depth profile). Use it, or extend it with an argument, instead of writing a second version for your feature.
  • If an existing helper is close but not quite right, change it in one place and update its callers, rather than copying it under a new name. #83 did this with a second bounds reader for buffers, which then had to be merged back.
  • Use the existing classes (SpatVoxel, SpatEnvelope, SpatVolume) and their constructors and converters (as_voxel(), as_envelope(), vect_to_envelope(), envelope_to_voxel()) instead of new structures for the same data.
  • Prefer existing dependencies (terra, sf, ncdf4) to hand-written geometry or file reading. Check the package does what you need before writing your own.
  • A new exported function, class or data representation needs a reason the existing ones can’t serve. Say what you checked in the PR description.

Internal helpers

Don’t create an internal function unless it earns its place (#97).

Keep a helper when:

  • it is called from several places, or
  • it holds real logic that is reused or likely to be (e.g. time decoding, great-circle distance), or
  • it is a clearly named unit with its own tests covering behaviour the exported function can’t easily reach.

Inline it when:

  • it has one call site and is short,
  • it only forwards its arguments to another function or wraps one base R call,
  • it is an if/else chain that picks a value or an error message for one caller,
  • it is one layer in a chain of single-use functions.

Large single-use steps (e.g. .extract_one_file()) can stay if they make the exported function read as a sequence of named steps.

When you inline a helper that tests call directly, move those checks onto the exported function rather than deleting them.

Conditions (errors, warnings, messages)

  • Signal classed conditions with rlang::abort(), rlang::warn() and rlang::inform() and a class = argument. Don’t build conditions by hand with structure(list(message = ..., call = NULL), class = c(...)).
  • Build messages with glue::glue() so values appear in place ("{n} observations have ...") instead of long paste0() chains. Work out plural wording in a variable first.
  • Condition classes are internal: they exist so tests can catch or silence a specific condition without matching its wording. Don’t document them in help pages, NEWS or README.
  • Name classes ocean3d_<error|warning|message>_<what> (e.g. ocean3d_warning_timezone). Some existing classes predate this convention; #97 renames them.
  • Attach data to a condition only if package code or a test reads it, and give each class a single producer with the same fields every time.
  • A helper that signals a condition is worth keeping when the condition is raised from several places. With one call site, signal it inline.

Tests

  • Test behaviour through the exported functions, on synthetic data (no external files, keys or network).
  • Check conditions with expect_error() / expect_warning() using class =, plus expect_match() on the parts of the message that matter.
  • Use skip_if_not_installed() only for packages in Suggests (e.g. lwgeom). Packages in Imports, such as ncdf4, are always installed, so a skip for them never triggers and only adds noise.

Docs

  • roxygen2 docs on every changed exported function. Run devtools::document(); never edit man/ or NAMESPACE by hand.
  • Follow the CONTRIBUTING.md “Coding conventions”, “Testing” and “Documentation and vignettes” sections; they aren’t repeated here.

Workflow

  • One agent per issue, on its own branch in its own git worktree, branched from up-to-date origin/main. Name branches <N>-<slug> or <type>/<N>-<slug> (e.g. 74-coordinate-axis-handling, docs/59-getting-started-vignette).
  • Put Closes #N in the PR body so the issue closes on merge. (#N) in the title is not enough.
  • Keep PRs reviewable in one sitting: about 400 changed lines in R/ and 1000 in total. Generated files (man/, NAMESPACE, renv.lock, rendered articles) don’t count. Split bigger work into PRs that each branch from main, do one thing and pass devtools::check(). Open the next one after the previous one merges (e.g. shared helpers, then the function, then articles). #83 (a 2100-line extract_to_buffer.R) is the example to avoid.
  • Don’t stack PRs (a PR whose base is another open PR’s branch). Every change to a lower PR has to be merged into and re-reviewed in each PR above it, which multiplies review work. Branch from main, and wait for the PR your work depends on to merge.
  • Agents can push their branch and open a PR for their issue. A person reviews every PR, and only the developer approves and squash-merges: don’t merge or approve. Don’t open issues or post comments elsewhere on GitHub unless the developer asks.
  • Each PR gets an agent code review and a prose review of its docs and text. Reply to each review comment with what changed and in which commit (e.g. “Fixed in e860cb3: …”).
  • Commits and PR descriptions written with an agent include AI attribution, e.g. a Co-Authored-By: trailer naming the model.
  • Before handing back: devtools::document(), devtools::test(), devtools::check(), and lintr::lint() on changed files with no new lints.
